## Email 1 — Prof. Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli

**To**: rafaelgb@mit.edu  
**Subject**: Exploring Collaboration: AI-Driven Catalyst Design between Beihang University and MIT

Dear Prof. Gómez-Bombarelli,

I hope this message finds you well. I am Yuzhou Liu, a Professor at the School of Chemistry, Beihang University (BUAA) in Beijing, China.

I recently read about your group's latest work on accelerating materials discovery with AI and simulations (MIT News, February 2026), as well as your pioneering efforts in combining physics-based simulations with generative AI for catalyst and polymer design. Your approach of fusing computational design with machine learning to bypass the traditional trial-and-error methodology is truly inspiring — and closely aligned with our research direction.

At Beihang University, our group has been actively working at the intersection of AI and catalysis. We have developed machine learning models for catalyst screening and reaction pathway prediction, with several publications in this emerging area. Given your group's leadership in AI-driven materials discovery and our expertise in catalytic systems, I believe there are compelling opportunities for collaboration, including:

1. **Joint research on AI-guided catalyst design** — combining your generative models with our experimental validation capabilities in heterogeneous catalysis
2. **Shared datasets and benchmarking** — establishing common benchmarks for AI model evaluation in catalysis
3. **Graduate student exchange** — fostering cross-cultural scientific training

I would be honored to share our recent representative publications with you, and I would welcome the opportunity to arrange a brief video call at your convenience to explore potential synergies.

Should your schedule permit in the future, we would also be delighted to welcome you to visit our laboratory at Beihang University.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to the possibility of working together.

Warm regards,

**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry  
Beihang University (北京航空航天大学)

## Email 2 — Prof. Elsa A. Olivetti

**To**: elsaol@mit.edu  
**Subject**: Collaboration Opportunity: AI for Sustainable Catalysis and Materials Lifecycle Analysis

Dear Prof. Olivetti,

I am writing to express my admiration for your groundbreaking work at the intersection of AI, materials science, and environmental sustainability. Your recent recognition with tenure at MIT DMSE (2026) and your leadership in the MIT Climate Project are truly commendable.

I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at the School of Chemistry, Beihang University, Beijing. My research group focuses on AI-assisted catalyst design and development, with a growing emphasis on the sustainability metrics of catalytic processes. Your work developing analytical and computational models to assess the cost and environmental impact of materials at early stages resonates deeply with our goals.

We have been developing machine learning frameworks that not only optimize catalytic performance but also incorporate life-cycle assessment (LCA) parameters — a methodology that draws heavily on approaches your group has pioneered. I believe a collaboration could be mutually beneficial in areas such as:

1. **AI-integrated LCA for catalyst design** — embedding sustainability metrics directly into ML-based catalyst screening pipelines
2. **Joint grant proposals** — targeting international funding for sustainable chemistry and AI
3. **Co-supervision of students** interested in sustainable AI-driven chemistry

I would appreciate the opportunity to share our recent work and discuss potential synergies. Please let me know if a brief introductory meeting might be possible.

Warm regards,

**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry  
Beihang University (北京航空航天大学)

## Email 4 — Prof. Mingda Li

**To**: mingda@mit.edu  
**Subject**: Exploring Synergies: Generative AI for Quantum and Catalytic Materials Design

Dear Prof. Li,

I am writing to express my enthusiasm for your group's recent breakthrough in using generative AI for quantum materials design, published in Nature Materials (September 2025). Your SCIGEN tool and the insight that "we don't need 10 million new materials to change the world — we just need one really good material" perfectly captures the philosophy we share.

I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at the School of Chemistry, Beihang University, Beijing. Our research group works at the interface of AI and catalysis, developing machine learning models that go beyond brute-force screening to target functionally optimal materials.

Your approach of steering generative AI models toward specific geometric lattice structures associated with quantum properties is fascinating. I believe similar principles could be transformative in catalytic materials design — where the goal is not stability alone, but specific active-site geometries and electronic structures. Potential collaboration areas include:

1. **Adapting generative AI frameworks** from quantum materials to catalytic materials design
2. **Joint exploration of design rules** for AI-generated functional materials
3. **Cross-validation** — testing AI-predicted catalytic materials experimentally in our lab

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these ideas with you and share our group's recent work.

Warm regards,

**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry  
Beihang University (北京航空航天大学)

## Email 6 — Elton Pan (cc: thesis advisor)

**To**: eltonpan@mit.edu  
**Subject**: Re: Your DiffSyn Work on AI-Guided Zeolite Synthesis — Potential Collaboration Interest

Dear Elton,

I hope this message finds you well. I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at the School of Chemistry, Beihang University, Beijing.

I read with great interest the recent MIT News coverage of your DiffSyn model for AI-guided zeolite synthesis (February 2026). Your approach of using generative AI to suggest promising synthesis routes — and successfully demonstrating it by synthesizing a new zeolite with improved thermal stability — is remarkable. Zeolites remain one of the most important classes of industrial catalysts, and your work addresses the exact bottleneck we face: knowing what we want to make but not how to make it.

At Beihang University, our group has extensive experience in zeolite-based catalytic systems and heterogeneous catalysis more broadly. We have also been exploring machine learning approaches for reaction condition optimization. I believe there is strong potential for collaboration:

1. **Extending DiffSyn concepts** to other catalytic material systems beyond zeolites
2. **Experimental validation partnership** — testing AI-predicted synthesis routes in our laboratory
3. **Joint methodology development** for AI-guided materials synthesis

I would be delighted to connect and discuss these possibilities. Please feel free to share this note with your advisor as well.

Best regards,

**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry  
Beihang University (北京航空航天大学)

## Email 7 — Mouyang Cheng (cc: thesis advisor)

**To**: mcheng@mit.edu  
**Subject**: Re: Your AI Model for Atomic Defect Characterization — Collaboration Interest from Beihang University

Dear Mouyang,

I hope this message finds you well. I am Yuzhou Liu, Professor at the School of Chemistry, Beihang University, Beijing.

I was very impressed by your recent work using AI to uncover atomic defects in materials via neutron-scattering techniques (MIT News, March 2026). The ability to simultaneously detect six different types of point defects in a material — something you rightly described as "unthinkable" with conventional techniques — is a remarkable achievement. Your use of multihead attention mechanisms, inspired by transformer architectures, to extract subtle differences across 2,000 semiconductor materials and 56 elements is truly innovative.

While our group at Beihang University focuses primarily on catalysis rather than semiconductors, the underlying AI methodology — particularly the foundational model approach that leverages multihead attention for materials characterization — has exciting potential applications in catalytic materials science. Understanding defect structures in catalytic materials is crucial for activity and selectivity optimization.

I would be interested in discussing:

1. **Transferring your AI defect characterization methodology** to catalytic material systems
2. **Collaborative publications** exploring AI-enabled materials characterization across domains
3. **Technical exchange** on multihead attention architectures for materials science

Please feel free to share this with your advisor. I would welcome a conversation.

Best regards,

**Yuzhou Liu (刘宇宙)**  
Professor, School of Chemistry  
Beihang University (北京航空航天大学)
